own_scenes.desc: La revolución social inspiró la revolución rítmica: James Brown demostró que se podía usar una banda entera como una batería y llevar los polirritmos de vuelta a África, y los músicos que habían tocado para que otros bailaran se pusieron a bailar ellos. A mediados de los sesenta el nuevo groove se notó en «Respect» de Otis Redding, «Uptight» de Stevie Wonder o «Shotgun» de Junior Walker. «Funky Broadway» (1967) de Dyke and the Blazers, de Phoenix, fue el primer disco de baile negro que se llamó funky; Wilson Pickett lo pulió en Muscle Shoals y llegó al número 1 de R&B. Joe Tex pasó de las baladas al R&B caliente y al funk lascivo («Skinny Legs and All», «I Gotcha»). En Los Ángeles, Charles Wright y su Watts 103rd Street Rhythm Band dieron un funk suave y elegante («Express Yourself», sampleado por N.W.A.). Grupos instrumentales se volvían bandas: los Jazziacs neoyorquinos serían Kool & the Gang; los Ohio Untouchables, los Ohio Players; los Creators de Compton, War.

refs.q: It was the social revolution in America that inspired the rhythm revolution.
refs.para: It was the social revolution in America that inspired the rhythm revolution. The desegregated mobility of black performers, their well-trained versatility, the playfulness and optimism of the times, and a profound sense of mission drew black musicians in the 1960s to combine and interrelate the many strands of their musical traditions, affirming them all, while creating still others. The inevitable musical cross-pollenation led to a celebration of the depth and breadth of the music—a music one was no longer ashamed to admit was rooted in Mother Africa. Sarah Brown and John Morthland describe the burgeoning proto-funk phenomenon in the liner notes to the 1994 compilation CD The Roots of Funk:

refs.q: The Phoenix-based Dyke and the Blazers kick-started the funky dance fad in early 1967
refs.para: The Phoenix-based Dyke and the Blazers kick-started the funky dance fad in early 1967, with “Funky Broadway—Part I.” A heaving, lumpy groove with a jumping bass and percussive organ, “Funky Broadway” was the first black dance record to call itself funky—and it was. Dyke’s scratchy lyrics celebrated the ubiquity of Broadways everywhere, as the gritty grimy feel of nightlife on the boulevard came to life. Originating in Buffalo, Dyke’s band was backing the O’Jays on a tour, but was stranded by the yet unsuccessful singers in Phoenix. (The group made the best of their funky situation until Arlester “Dyke” Christian was shot to death in Phoenix in 1971.)
